descriptor.scene: There is no human being in this frame and NO second mascot figure of any kind: the manager is the ONLY glowing figure and the ONLY capped figure in this picture. The camera is well back inside the glowing machine; the MACHINES are the subject and the manager rides through them. A wide honey-wood CHUTE runs diagonally through the middle of the frame from upper left to lower right, its sides open like a flume, brass rails inside it. The manager rides down it standing on a small cream carriage, at full length and no taller than a third of the frame height, turned three-quarter with one mitten arm raised, head up, weight forward, his plum light streaking the chute walls behind him. The chute feeds two large machines that read clearly as two separate named machines. At the RIGHT, a big old well-polished machine of dark honeyed wood and worn brass, plainly built long ago and cared for ever since, its wide mouth open, one finished picture book resting inside it in warm lamplight. At the UPPER LEFT, a taller cream machine with a row of small round brass-rimmed windows down its side. Behind EVERY one of those windows hangs the SAME SMALL PAINTED PORTRAIT of one ordinary human child, an ink-and-wash painting on cream paper of a boy of about five with brown hair, repeated identically window after window so the sameness is the point. Those are FLAT PAINTED PICTURES pinned behind glass: not creatures, not mascots, not glowing, no plum bodies, no dot eyes and no caps of any kind anywhere in those windows. Warm honeyed light throughout, plum glow only along the chute and around the manager. Composition: tall cream machine upper left, chute and manager through the centre, old wooden machine lower right; the top right stays calm warm wall.
descriptor._caption: He cannot take a single step without that step's machine, and he would not want to. The reader was built once and polished for years. The character shop keeps every face the same, book after book. His job is never to remake what the factory already knows. His job is to choose the way through it.
